what_it_does: Large language models generate text one word (token) at a time, and a technique called 'early exiting' tries to stop processing partway through the network when the model is already confident about its answer — saving computation. The bottleneck is a small gatekeeper program that must scan a vocabulary of roughly 30,000 possible next tokens at every layer of the network to decide whether to exit early, and this scanning alone eats up to 20% of total inference time. SpecEE fixes this by using a tiny 'draft' model (a much smaller language model) to pre-screen the vocabulary and hand the gatekeeper a short list of plausible candidates instead of all 30,000, so the gatekeeper's job becomes far cheaper. The system also profiles how often each layer of the main network actually triggers an early exit and deploys the gatekeeper unevenly — spending more effort on the layers where it matters most. A special tree-aware mapping lets SpecEE work alongside 'speculative decoding' (a separate trick where multiple candidate continuations are processed simultaneously as a tree), without the combination exploding in complexity.
